lesson.title: Why a Strong r Does Not Tell the Whole Story
lesson.summary: Correlation only measures straight line association, can be dragged around by a single outlier, and even a very strong r never proves that one variable causes the other.
lesson.body:
A correlation coefficient is a powerful summary, but it summarizes only one thing: straight line association. Trusting r without checking the conditions behind it, or without asking what else might explain a pattern, is one of the most common statistical mistakes, and it is worth walking through exactly how it happens, in three distinct ways.

The first limitation is that r is blind to strong relationships that are not linear. Take five points where y equals the squared distance of x from 3: at x equal to 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, y equals 4, 1, 0, 1, 4. This is a perfect U-shaped relationship, y is completely determined by x with no scatter at all, yet computing r gives exactly 0. The deviations above and below the mean of x pair up with the deviations above and below the mean of y in a way that the positive and negative products cancel out entirely, five products of negative 4, 1, 0, negative 1, and 4 that sum to zero. A relationship can be as strong and predictable as possible and still produce r near zero if its form is curved rather than straight, which is exactly why the form of a scatterplot is always checked visually before r is trusted as a summary.

The second limitation is that r is sensitive to individual outliers, especially in small data sets. Starting again from the five students with r about 0.99, add a sixth student who studied 6 hours but scored only 20 points, perhaps due to illness or test anxiety, badly breaking the established pattern. Recomputing correlation across all six points drops r from about 0.99 down to about negative 0.10, a swing from strong positive association to essentially no linear association at all, caused by a single unusual point among six. A correlation computed on a small data set can be dominated by one influential observation, so any reported r should always be checked against the actual scatterplot for outliers before it is trusted or repeated.

The third and most important limitation is that correlation, no matter how strong, never by itself establishes causation. A classic illustration: across the months of the year, ice cream sales and drowning deaths are strongly positively correlated. Neither one causes the other, nobody drowns because someone bought ice cream, and nobody buys ice cream because a drowning occurred. Both are driven by a third, lurking variable, warm weather, which independently sends more people swimming, raising drowning risk, and sends more people to buy ice cream to cool off. Whenever two variables turn out to be correlated, a careful statistician asks whether one could plausibly cause the other, or whether both might instead be responses to some shared underlying cause that was never measured.

Taken together, these three limitations point to the same habit: always look at the scatterplot itself, check whether the pattern is really linear before trusting a correlation, look for points that do not belong, and think hard about what else could explain an association before concluding that one variable drives the other.
